Statement-combination
A principal-protected note invests RM200,000 and pays 50% participation in a 8% underlying gain. Estimate total maturity proceeds before costs and tax.
Maturity proceeds = protected principal + (principal × participation rate × underlying gain).

Answer: B — RM208,000.
Why this is correct:
Formula: Maturity proceeds = protected principal + (principal × participation rate × underlying gain).
Working:
Participation-linked return = RM200,000 × 50% × 8% = RM8,000. Maturity proceeds = RM200,000 + RM8,000 = RM208,000.
Why the other options are wrong:
A — RM204,000: uses the principal only, applies the full underlying gain without participation, or treats the return as the total proceeds.
C — RM200,000: uses the principal only, applies the full underlying gain without participation, or treats the return as the total proceeds.
D — RM216,000: uses the principal only, applies the full underlying gain without participation, or treats the return as the total proceeds.
Exam cue: For principal-protected participation payoffs, calculate the upside return, then add it to principal.

Approximate YTM = [annual coupon + (par − price) ÷ years to maturity] ÷ [(par + price) ÷ 2] × 100.

An investor pays RM97,000 for a discount security that matures at RM100,000 in 180 days. Estimate the annualised yield.
Annualised return = (redemption value − purchase price) ÷ purchase price × 365 ÷ days held × 100.

Answer: C — 6.27%.

Why this is correct:
Formula: Annualised return = (redemption value − purchase price) ÷ purchase price × 365 ÷ days held × 100.

Working:
Profit = RM100,000 − RM97,000 = RM3,000. Holding-period return = RM3,000 ÷ RM97,000 = 3.09%. Annualised return = 3.09% × 365 ÷ 180 = 6.27% per annum.

Why the other options are wrong:
A — 6.08%: uses only the holding-period return, omits annualisation, or divides by the wrong base.
B — 3.09%: uses only the holding-period return, omits annualisation, or divides by the wrong base.
D — 7.27%: uses only the holding-period return, omits annualisation, or divides by the wrong base.

Exam cue: For discount securities, the return is earned through the difference between purchase price and redemption value.

A put option on Bond Z has a strike price of RM100 per RM100 face value (i.e., at par) and expires in 3 months. The bond is currently trading at RM97. Is this put option in-the-money, at-the-money, or out-of-the-money? What is the intrinsic value?
Out-of-the-money; intrinsic value = RM0.
At-the-money; intrinsic value = RM0.
In-the-money; intrinsic value = RM3 per RM100 face value.
In-the-money; intrinsic value = RM103.
Put intrinsic value = max(strike price − current price, 0).

Answer: C — In-the-money; intrinsic value = RM3 per RM100 face value.

Why this is correct:
Formula: Put intrinsic value = max(strike price − current price, 0).

Working:
The put allows the holder to sell at RM100 when the bond is trading at RM97. Intrinsic value = max(RM100 − RM97, 0) = RM3 per RM100 face value, so it is in-the-money.

Why the other options are wrong:
A — Out-of-the-money; intrinsic value = RM0: treats the option as out-of-the-money, ignores the strike-current price difference, or adds the two prices together.
B — At-the-money; intrinsic value = RM0: treats the option as out-of-the-money, ignores the strike-current price difference, or adds the two prices together.
D — In-the-money; intrinsic value = RM103: treats the option as out-of-the-money, ignores the strike-current price difference, or adds the two prices together.

Exam cue: A put is in-the-money when the strike price is above the current underlying price.

A structured product's term sheet states: 'Protection Level: 90%; Participation Rate: 130%; Reference Asset: FBM KLCI; Tenor: 5 years.' An investor invests RM200,000. The KLCI falls 15% over 5 years. What does the investor receive at maturity?

RM170,000; the 15% fall is deducted from principal.
RM180,000; the 90% protection floor applies and no upside return is earned.
RM161,000; 130% of the 15% fall is applied to principal.
Protected floor = principal × protection level.

Answer: C — RM180,000; the 90% protection floor applies and no upside return is earned.
Why this is correct:
Formula: Protected floor = principal × protection level.
Working:
RM200,000 × 90% = RM180,000. Because the reference asset falls, there is no positive participation return, so the protected floor applies.
Why the other options are wrong:
A — RM200,000; full principal is protected: assumes full principal protection or applies the participation rate to the loss.
B — RM170,000; the 15% fall is deducted from principal: assumes full principal protection or applies the participation rate to the loss.
D — RM161,000; 130% of the 15% fall is applied to principal: assumes full principal protection or applies the participation rate to the loss.
Exam cue: Read the protection level separately from the participation rate.

A 5-year corporate bond has a face value of RM1,000 and pays an annual coupon of 4.0%. It is currently priced at RM930. Using the approximate YTM formula, what is the approximate yield to maturity?

Answer: A — 5.60%.

Why this is correct:
Formula: Approximate YTM = [annual coupon + (par − price) ÷ years to maturity] ÷ [(par + price) ÷ 2] × 100.

Working:
Annual coupon = RM1,000 × 4.0% = RM40. Annual capital gain = (RM1,000 − RM930) ÷ 5 = RM14. Average price = (RM1,000 + RM930) ÷ 2 = RM965. Approximate YTM = (RM40 + RM14) ÷ RM965 × 100 = 5.60%.

Why the other options are wrong:
B — 4.30%: uses only the coupon rate, ignores the discount accretion to par, or overstates the annual capital gain.
C — 6.36%: uses only the coupon rate, ignores the discount accretion to par, or overstates the annual capital gain.

Using a 365-day year, calculate the annualised return for buying at RM97,000 and redeeming at RM100,000 after 90 days.
Approximately 3.00% per annum.
Approximately 12.54% per annum.
Approximately 3.09% per annum.
Approximately 0.76% per annum.
Annualised return = (redemption value − purchase price) ÷ purchase price × 365 ÷ days held × 100.

Answer: B — Approximately 12.54% per annum.
Why this is correct:
Formula: Annualised return = (redemption value − purchase price) ÷ purchase price × 365 ÷ days held × 100.
Working:
Profit = RM100,000 − RM97,000 = RM3,000. Holding-period return = RM3,000 ÷ RM97,000 = 3.09%. Annualised return = 3.09% × 365 ÷ 90 = 12.54% per annum.
Why the other options are wrong:
A — Approximately 3.00% per annum: uses only the holding-period return, omits annualisation, or divides by the redemption value instead of the purchase price.
C — Approximately 3.09% per annum: uses only the holding-period return, omits annualisation, or divides by the redemption value instead of the purchase price.
D — Approximately 0.76% per annum: uses only the holding-period return, omits annualisation, or divides by the redemption value instead of the purchase price.
Exam cue: For discount securities, calculate the profit first, then annualise it over the holding period.
